The God You Could Love

# The God You Could Love

### The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad turned the impersonal Absolute into a personal God, and was the first Upaniṣad to speak of Bhakti.

Śvetāśvatara, the sage who signed this Upaniṣad, means "the one with white horses.” Image: Helena Lopes.

Most of the famous Upaniṣads open in the middle of a conversation. In the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, a boy named Naciketas badgers Death himself about what survives the body. In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, the sage Yājñavalkya spars with a king in open court, and, elsewhere in that same Upaniṣad, tries to explain the self to his wife Maitreyī before he leaves home for good. The Śvetāśvatara opens differently. It opens with a seminar.

A circle of men described as **Brahmavādins**, people who discuss **Brahman**, the ultimate reality behind the world, are sitting together and they put a question on the table:

> *kiṃ kāraṇaṃ brahma kutaḥ sma jātā*  
> *jīvāma kena kva ca saṃpratiṣṭhāḥ*  
> *adhiṣṭhitāḥ kena sukhetareṣu*  
> *vartāmahe brahmavido vyavasthām*
>
> “What is the cause? Is it brahman? From where were we born? By what do
> we live, and where do we come to rest? Governed by whom do we live out
> our lives in pleasure and in pain, you who know brahman?” (1.1)

Then they run through the possible answers one by one:

> *kālaḥ svabhāvo niyatir yadṛcchā*  
> *bhūtāni yoniḥ puruṣa iti cintyā*
>
> “Time, inherent nature, necessity, chance, the elements, the womb of
> things, the person: so runs the inquiry.” (1.2)

Is the cause of everything time? Is it **Svabhāva**, the inherent nature of things? Is it necessity, or chance, or the basic physical elements, or **Puruṣa**, the conscious person? The Upaniṣad runs through the theories the early Indian thinkers actually argued over, and then it gives an answer that almost no other Upaniṣad gives in quite this voice:

> *te dhyānayogānugatā apaśyan*  
> *devātmaśaktiṃ svaguṇair nigūḍhām*  
> *yaḥ kāraṇāni nikhilāni tāni*  
> *kālātmayuktāny adhitiṣṭhaty ekaḥ*
>
> “The sages, absorbed in meditation, saw the self power of God, hidden
> by its own qualities. He, the One, alone presides over all those
> causes, from time to the self.” (1.3)

That answer tells you what kind of Upaniṣad you are holding. The sages who went deep in meditation found, behind time and nature and chance and the self, a single creative power that belongs to a **Deva**, a god. The word the verse gives that power, **Devātmaśakti**, the divine’s own power, is the earliest appearance of a term that the later traditions of the Goddess would treasure. And the cause turns out to be a person. One God, who stands behind all the impersonal candidates the seminar had listed, and rules them.

The Śvetāśvatara is a short Upaniṣad, six chapters of verse, and it is the one where the impersonal Absolute of the older Upaniṣads becomes a personal God, an **Īśvara**, a Lord with a will and a face, who creates, who rules, who hides inside every being, and who can be loved. It is the Upaniṣad that the later devotional traditions, both the worshippers of Śiva and the worshippers of Viṣṇu, would reach for again and again, because it is the place in the oldest layer of Indian scripture where philosophy and devotion are already fused. Almost everything that Hinduism becomes over the next two thousand years, the personal God or **Īśvara**, the practice of meditative yoga, the devotee’s surrender to the Lord, the doctrine of grace, the union of reason and love, is already here in seed. This is a guide to that Upaniṣad: to what its verses actually say, to the people who have spent their lives translating it, and to why the three great schools of Vedānta could read the very same lines and walk away with three different Gods.

A note on how to read along. I give the famous verses in the original, in transliteration, with a plain translation beneath, because the Śvetāśvatara is a text where the choice of an English word is often a choice of theology, and a reader who can see the Sanskrit sitting under the English is in a far better position to judge. The Sanskrit terms get explained the first time they appear. And the scholars and teachers I lean on, the philologists Max Müller, Patrick Olivelle, and Signe Cohen, the philosopher Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, and the three founding masters of Vedānta, Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, and Madhva, get introduced before I put words in their mouths.

## The Upaniṣad signs its own name

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Start with something the Śvetāśvatara does that no other classical Upaniṣad does. It tells you who wrote it.

The Upaniṣads are, as a rule, anonymous. They are named for the schools of recitation that preserved them, or for a teacher inside the story, and the actual composers stay invisible, which suited a tradition that liked to present its wisdom as timeless and authorless, breathed out with the Veda itself. The Śvetāśvatara breaks the pattern. Near the very end, in the verse numbered 6.21, it names its author:

> *tapaḥprabhāvād devaprasādāc ca*  
> *brahma ha śvetāśvataro ‘tha vidvān*  
> *atyāśramibhyaḥ paramaṃ pavitraṃ*  
> *provāca samyag ṛṣisaṃghajuṣṭam*
>
> “Through the power of his austerity and through the grace of God, the
> wise Śvetāśvatara rightly proclaimed brahman, the supreme and holy, to
> the most advanced renouncers, and it was welcomed by the company of
> seers.” (6.21)

The Upaniṣad is named after a man, and the man is named inside it. Signe Cohen, an American scholar of Sanskrit whose 2008 book *Text and Authority in the Older Upaniṣads* is one of the more careful modern studies of how these texts were built, makes this her starting point. **Cohen's point is that the Śvetāśvatara is the only one of the classical Upaniṣads ascribed to an individual, historical author, a named person rather than a school of recitation.** The name itself is debated, and its two natural readings pull in different directions. Split one way, as śveta plus aśvatara, the ordinary Sanskrit word for a mule, it means "the one with white mules," which is how the standard lexicon sees it. Split the other way, as śvetāśva, white horse, plus a suffix, it points to white horses instead. Some scholars even take the name as that of a Vedic school rather than a man. Tradition reads it as the personal name of the sage, and some later interpreters heard in it a symbol of purified senses, though that gloss is devotional embroidery rather than settled philology. Whoever he was, he wanted his name on the work.

By Cohen’s analysis this signature belongs to the oldest layer of the text. The impulse to claim personal authorship was there from the start. This is a composer who wanted you to know that a particular person, by a particular discipline and a particular gift of grace, had come to see the **Deva**, the God, and was now telling you about it. The Upaniṣad is, in that sense, a testimony, and notice that the very signature verse already contains the two ideas the whole work will live by: austerity, the seeker’s effort, and **Devaprasāda**, the grace of God. Effort and grace, named together, in the line where the author signs his name.

## How old is it?

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Before going further into what the Upaniṣad teaches, it helps to know roughly when it was speaking, because the Śvetāśvatara is usually filed among the later principal Upaniṣads, and it is worth seeing exactly what that does and does not mean.

Patrick Olivelle, whose 1998 critical edition and translation, *The Early Upaniṣads*, is the standard scholarly text in English, places it after the Kaṭha and the Īśā and before the Muṇḍaka, and dates it, with appropriate caution, to “the last few centuries BCE.” He quotes the German scholar Thomas Oberlies to the effect that it can hardly have been composed long before the first century before the common era.

Cohen complicates that judgment in a way worth slowing down for, because it changes how you read the whole thing. Rather than date the text as a single block, she dates its layers. Old Indian verse comes in different metres, and the metres carry chronological fingerprints. Most of the Śvetāśvatara is composed in the older, looser metres called *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī*, the same metrical world as the oldest Upaniṣads. Running through it is a second layer in the tighter, later *śloka* metre, the classical verse form, and that layer often reads like a teacher’s explanatory gloss that has been absorbed into the text and now sits right beside the verse it was explaining. Her conclusion is careful: the core was “composed around the same time as some of the oldest Upaniṣads, but likely later than the very oldest,” and what we now hold is a work that grew in layers over a long stretch of time. She is insistent that we are reading the “extant version,” the text as it ended up, not some pristine original.

So the answer to “how old is the Śvetāśvatara” is that it has an old heart inside a body that kept growing. The questions about the cause of the world, the vision of the one God, the signature of the sage, these belong to the deep layer. Some of the more systematic philosophical verses came later. **Putting the evidence together, a defensible working date for the Śvetāśvatara as we have it is roughly 400 to 200 BCE, with a core that may reach back further still.** Olivelle himself warns that any attempt to date these documents more precisely than a few centuries is, in his phrase, “as stable as a house of cards,” so a range, and not a single year, is the honest answer. Read this way, the occasional unevenness of the Upaniṣad’s surface stops being a puzzle and becomes a record of how a living tradition kept thinking with the same short scripture for centuries.

## The one God

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FqFh!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcf69290b-a502-4145-898a-6023eab19a79_985x1597.png)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FqFh!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcf69290b-a502-4145-898a-6023eab19a79_985x1597.png)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Three-headed Shiva, Gandhara, 2nd century AD.

At the center of the Śvetāśvatara stands a God, and everything distinctive about the Upaniṣad flows from him.

The older Upaniṣads are famous for an impersonal vision of the ultimate. Brahman, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and the Chāndogya, is reality itself, consciousness without a second, approached by stripping away every limited description until only the bare “not this, not this” remains. It is the ground of being, and it is identical with your own deepest self, the ***Ā*****tman**, but it is not a person you pray to. The Śvetāśvatara keeps all of that metaphysical depth and gives the Absolute a face.

The face it gives is **Rudra**, the fierce Vedic god of storm and wild places who would later be worshipped as Śiva. The Upaniṣad is emphatic about his oneness:

> *eko hi rudro na dvitīyāya tasthur*  
> *ya imāṃl lokān īśata īśanībhiḥ*  
> *pratyaṅ janāṃs tiṣṭhati sañcukocānta-*  
> *kāle saṃsṛjya viśvā bhuvanāni gopāḥ*
>
> “Rudra is truly one; they did not allow a second. He rules these
> worlds by his ruling powers. He stands facing all beings; having
> created all the worlds, he, the protector, draws them back at the end
> of time.” (3.2)

There is a deliberate insistence here, a hammering on the word *one*, that Olivelle notices and names. A major aim of the author, he writes, is “to establish that the God who creates and from whom one expects salvation is one,” and the Upaniṣad drives this home by repeating the little word **Eka**, one, again and again. This is one supreme God who has gathered up all the functions the older texts had spread across an impersonal Absolute and a crowd of deities.

And this God is described in language of startling reach. He is the great **Puruṣa**, the cosmic Person, sunlike, and to know him is to pass beyond death. This is one of the most chanted verses in the whole tradition:

> *vedāham etaṃ puruṣaṃ mahāntam*  
> *ādityavarṇaṃ tamasaḥ parastāt*  
> *tam eva viditvāti mṛtyum eti*  
> *nānyaḥ panthā vidyate ‘yanāya*
>
> “I know that great Person, the color of the sun, beyond the darkness.
> Only by knowing him does one go beyond death. There is no other path
> to go.” (3.8)

That last line, *nānyaḥ panthā vidyate ‘yanāya*, “there is no other path,” became a stock formula of the whole liberation tradition. We will come back to this verse, because it carries a secret about where the Śvetāśvatara found its material.

The God of this Upaniṣad is also described through paradox, in a verse that became the model for a whole style of negative theology:

> *apāṇipādo javano grahītā*  
> *paśyaty acakṣuḥ sa śṛṇoty akarṇaḥ*  
> *sa vetti vedyaṃ na ca tasyāsti vettā*  
> *tam āhur agryaṃ puruṣaṃ mahāntam*
>
> “Without hands and feet, he moves swiftly and grasps; he sees without
> eyes, he hears without ears. He knows whatever can be known, but of
> him there is no knower. They call him the foremost, the great Person.”
> (3.19)

And, most expansively of all, this God is every gender and every age, present in all things:

> *tvaṃ strī tvaṃ pumān asi*  
> *tvaṃ kumāra uta vā kumārī*  
> *tvaṃ jīrṇo daṇḍena vañcasi*  
> *tvaṃ jāto bhavasi viśvatomukhaḥ*
>
> “You are woman, you are man; you are the youth and also the maiden.
> You, grown old, totter along on a staff; you, once born, come to be
> facing in every direction.” (4.3)

Most beautiful of all, in the line that gives this essay its title, he is hidden:

> *eko devaḥ sarvabhūteṣu gūḍhaḥ*  
> *sarvavyāpī sarvabhūtāntarātmā*  
> *karmādhyakṣaḥ sarvabhūtādhivāsaḥ*  
> *sākṣī cetā kevalo nirguṇaś ca*
>
> “The one God, hidden in all beings, all pervading, the inner self of
> all beings, overseer of all action, dwelling in all beings, the
> witness, the conscious one, alone, and beyond all qualities.” (6.11)

*Eko devaḥ sarvabhūteṣu gūḍhaḥ.* The one God, concealed in everything that exists, present in you as your own innermost witness. The Absolute has not vanished. It has been given a personal face, and the ground of being is now someone who sees you. Notice the last line of that verse, where a single God is called both **Sākṣī**, the witness, and **Nirguṇa**, beyond qualities. In one breath the Upaniṣad holds together the warm personal God of devotion and the attributeless Absolute of the philosophers, and that double grip is exactly why every later school could find itself here.

## The borrowed jewels

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Here is one of the most interesting things about the Śvetāśvatara, and one that popular accounts almost never mention. Some of its most famous verses are not original to it. The Upaniṣad is quoting older scripture, and once you know where to look, the seams are visible, and they tell a story.

Take that great verse 3.8, “I know that great Person, the color of the sun.” It feels like the heart of the Upaniṣad, and it is, but it did not begin there. It is a verse from the later layer of the **Puruṣa Sūkta**, the ancient hymn of the cosmic Person, transmitted in the Yajurveda, in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, and in the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad. A small correction worth making, because popular sources blur it: this verse is not from the original Ṛgvedic Puruṣa Sūkta of book ten. It belongs to the appended verses preserved in the Yajurveda recensions. The Śvetāśvatara took an old liturgical jewel and set it into its own crown.

The same is true, even more strikingly, of the most famous image in the entire Upaniṣad, the two birds, which we will read in full in a moment. That verse is word for word identical to a verse of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad, and both of them reproduce, syllable for syllable, a verse of the Ṛgveda itself, the riddle hymn of book one. A single image traveled from the oldest Indian poetry, through the Muṇḍaka, into the Śvetāśvatara, unchanged.

And then there is a quieter borrowing that shows the Śvetāśvatara’s hand more clearly than any other. One of the most quoted lines in all of Hindu scripture is the paradox of the divine size, smaller than the smallest and larger than the largest. The Śvetāśvatara has it:

> *aṇor aṇīyān mahato mahīyān*  
> *ātmā guhāyāṃ nihito ‘sya jantoḥ*  
> *tam akratuḥ paśyati vītaśoko*  
> *dhātuḥ prasādān mahimānam īśam*
>
> “Smaller than the small, greater than the great, the self is set in
> the secret cave of the heart of this creature. The one without
> craving, freed from sorrow, beholds by the grace of the Ordainer the
> majesty, the Lord.” (3.20)

This verse also appears, almost identically, in the older Kaṭha Upaniṣad. The two are the same for three of their four lines. But the Śvetāśvatara changes the final word. Where the Kaṭha ends by saying that the seeker beholds “the greatness of the self,” *mahimānam ātmanaḥ*, the Śvetāśvatara ends by saying he beholds “the majesty, the Lord,” *mahimānam īśam*. One word is swapped, and an impersonal verse about the self becomes a theistic verse about a personal Lord. That single substitution is the whole project of the Śvetāśvatara in miniature. It inherits the meditative depth of the older Upaniṣads and turns it, gently and deliberately, toward a God.

So the Śvetāśvatara is, among other things, a great anthologist. It gathers the inherited jewels of the tradition, the cosmic Person from the Yajurveda, the two birds from the Ṛgveda and the Muṇḍaka, the size paradox from the Kaṭha, and it resets each one in a frame where the ultimate reality has a face and a name. The borrowing is not a weakness. It is the method. The Upaniṣad is showing you that the God it proclaims was there in the oldest scripture all along, waiting to be recognized.

## Two birds on one tree

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Now to that most beloved image, and to the place where the great schools of Vedānta divide.

> *dvā suparṇā sayujā sakhāyā*  
> *samānaṃ vṛkṣaṃ pariṣasvajāte*  
> *tayor anyaḥ pippalaṃ svādv atty*  
> *anaśnann anyo abhicākaśīti*
>
> “Two birds, companions ever joined, cling to the same tree. One of the
> two eats the sweet fruit; the other, not eating, looks on.” (4.6)
>
> *samāne vṛkṣe puruṣo nimagno*  
> *‘nīśayā śocati muhyamānaḥ*  
> *juṣṭaṃ yadā paśyaty anyam īśam asya*  
> *mahimānam iti vītaśokaḥ*
>
> “On the same tree the person, sunk in matter, grieves, deluded by his
> own powerlessness. But when he sees the other, the Lord, worshipped,
> and his greatness, then his grief passes away.” (4.7)

Two birds in one tree. One eats the fruit of experience, its pleasures and pains. The other simply watches, serene, tasting nothing. And the liberation of the grieving soul comes when it lifts its eyes to the watching bird and recognizes its glory. The image is so vivid, and so old, that every school of Vedānta claimed it and built on it, and the question they fought over is simple to state: who exactly are the two birds, and how are they related?

The eighth century master **Śaṅkara**, founder of **Advaita**, the school of pure nonduality, reads the two birds as the individual soul and God, and then dissolves the distance between them. Commenting on the same verse where it appears in the Muṇḍaka, he says the first bird, the individual soul, eats the fruits of pleasure and pain “owing to non discrimination,” while the second, God, “merely by his presence as the eternal witness,” tastes nothing and directs everything, the way a king presides without acting. And liberation, for Śaṅkara, is the moment the soul realizes that the two birds were never truly two. The soul sees the witness and understands, “I am this One who is the self of all,” and that the eating, suffering self was a misperception. For Advaita, the duality is a teaching device that points beyond itself to a final identity. In the end there is one bird.

The eleventh century teacher **Rāmānuja**, founder of **Viśiṣṭādvaita**, the school of qualified nonduality, reads the same image and stops short of that last step. For him the two birds are the soul and God, and they remain two, but they are inseparable, joined as a body is joined to the self that animates it. The soul is real and forever distinct, yet it has no existence apart from the God who is its inner ruler. Liberation is the soul, still itself, resting at last in loving nearness to a God who was always its support, rather than any discovery that the soul was God all along. There are two birds, bound together, forever.

The thirteenth century teacher **Madhva**, founder of **Dvaita**, the school of pure dualism, reads the two birds and keeps them fully and eternally apart. For Madhva the soul and God are different in the way light is different from the source of light, dependent but never identical, and the dependence itself, and the love that flows along it, is eternal. The soul never becomes God, in bondage or in liberation. There are two birds, and they are two forever.

One image, and three destinations for the soul. The Śvetāśvatara gives you the tree and the birds and the moment of looking up, and leaves the tradition to argue, for more than a thousand years, about what the soul sees when it looks. This is the Upaniṣad doing what it does best. It hands you a picture vivid enough to carry the weight of an entire philosophy, and old enough that all three schools can honestly claim it.

There is a detail here that almost no one outside the specialist literature mentions, and it is worth pausing on. None of these three great teachers actually wrote a surviving, accepted commentary on the Śvetāśvatara itself. There is a commentary on it that circulates under Śaṅkara’s name, but modern scholarship, most thoroughly in a 2018 study by Ivan Andrijanić, judges it the work of a later hand, because its vocabulary reflects developments in Advaita thought that came after Śaṅkara and it quotes texts younger than he was. Rāmānuja wrote no verse by verse commentary on any Upaniṣad. Madhva commented on ten Upaniṣads, and the Śvetāśvatara is not among them. What we have instead is something more revealing: all three traditions reached into this one short Upaniṣad and pulled out the verses they needed, and read the two birds through the lens of their own systems. The Śvetāśvatara was not so much commented upon as quarried.

## The meeting of the schools

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The Śvetāśvatara is also a crossroads of philosophies, and learning to see them is part of the pleasure of reading it.

That opening list of candidate causes, time and nature and necessity and chance, is a snapshot of the live philosophical debates of the day, and two of the systems it engages leave deep marks on its language. The first is **Sāṃkhya**, the analytical philosophy that explains the world as the interplay of two ultimate principles, **puruṣa**, pure consciousness, and **prakṛti**, primal matter, which unfolds into everything through the mixing of its three strands or **guṇas**. The second is **Yoga**, the discipline of stilling body and mind to reach liberating insight.

The Sāṃkhya vocabulary surfaces most famously in a verse that puzzled commentators for centuries:

> *ajām ekāṃ lohitaśuklakṛṣṇāṃ*  
> *bahvīḥ prajāḥ sṛjamānāṃ sarūpāḥ*  
> *ajo hy eko juṣamāṇo ‘nuśete*  
> *jahāty enāṃ bhuktabhogām ajo ‘nyaḥ*
>
> “There is one unborn female, red and white and black, giving birth to
> many creatures like herself. One unborn male lies by her and enjoys
> her; another unborn male leaves her once his enjoyment is done.” (4.5)

The red, white, and black female who gives birth to the world is read as **prakṛti**, nature, with her three **guṇas**, and the two unborn males as two souls, one bound to her and one free. The whole verse is a riddle in the Sāṃkhya key. The Upaniṣad even names the legendary founder of that system:

> *yo yoniṃ yonim adhitiṣṭhaty eko*  
> *viśvāni rūpāṇi yonīś ca sarvāḥ*  
> *ṛṣiṃ prasūtaṃ kapilaṃ yas tam agre*  
> *jñānair bibharti jāyamānaṃ ca paśyet*
>
> “The One who presides over each and every womb, over all forms and all
> sources, who bore the seer Kapila, born at the beginning, and watched
> over him as he was being born.” (5.2)

Whether **Kapila** here means the philosopher Kapila, the founder of Sāṃkhya, or simply means “tawny” and points to a golden cosmic being, is one of those genuinely open questions the readers handle differently, and we will see the divide in a moment. What is not in doubt is that the Upaniṣad is in living conversation with named schools of thought.

It also contains some of the oldest practical instructions for yoga meditation anywhere in the Upaniṣads:

> *trir unnataṃ sthāpya samaṃ śarīraṃ*  
> *hṛdīndriyāṇi manasā sanniveśya*  
> *brahmoḍupena pratareta vidvān*  
> *srotāṃsi sarvāṇi bhayānakāni*
>
> “Holding the body steady, with the three upper parts erect and even,
> drawing the senses and the mind into the heart, the wise man should
> cross all the fearful currents by the raft of brahman.” (2.8)

This is the classic posture verse, the seated, upright spine of meditation, and the yoga it teaches is **Dhyāna**, absorption, supported by restraint of the breath and the senses, the meditative kind rather than the postural gymnastics the word suggests today. It comes centuries before **Patañjali** gathered such practices into the systematic eight limbed yoga of the *Yoga Sūtras*, a work current scholarship places around the fourth or fifth century of the common era, well after this Upaniṣad. And the thread the Śvetāśvatara strikes here, meditation turned toward a personal Lord, is one Patañjali would keep: among his disciplines is **Īśvarapraṇidhāna**, surrender to the Lord. The same posture verse is echoed almost exactly in the Bhagavad Gītā’s instruction to hold the body, head, and neck straight and still. The Śvetāśvatara sits at the headwaters of the yoga tradition as surely as it does the devotional one.

But notice what the Śvetāśvatara does with the philosophy it borrows. Sāṃkhya, in its classic form, has no God. It explains the world through two impersonal principles and leaves it there. The Śvetāśvatara takes the whole Sāṃkhya apparatus and sets a personal Lord above it, a God who wields **prakṛti** rather than merely standing beside it. The dualism of consciousness and matter is kept as a description of the world, and then both are gathered under one God who is their source and ruler. The Upaniṣad is doing theology with the tools of philosophy, and it is among the earliest texts to do it so fully.

That theology reaches its high point in two verses that the later schools would never stop quoting. The first describes a God who acts without effort or instrument:

> *na tasya kāryaṃ karaṇaṃ ca vidyate*  
> *na tatsamaś cābhyadhikaś ca dṛśyate*  
> *parāsya śaktir vividhaiva śrūyate*  
> *svābhāvikī jñānabalakriyā ca*
>
> “Of him there is no work to be done and no instrument of action. No
> one is seen equal to him or greater. His supreme power is heard to be
> manifold, and natural, expressing itself as knowledge, strength, and
> action.” (6.8)

That last phrase, the threefold natural power of knowledge and strength and action, **jñāna bala kriyā**, became a technical foundation of later theology, the way the worshippers of Viṣṇu and the worshippers of Śiva alike would describe the inner life of God. The second is the verse that the dualist schools would make their banner, and we turn to it next.

## The God of the philosophers and the difference of souls

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

There is a verse near the end of the Śvetāśvatara that became one of the single most important proof texts in all of Vedānta, especially for the schools that insist the soul and God are permanently distinct.

> *nityo nityānāṃ cetanaś cetanānām*  
> *eko bahūnāṃ yo vidadhāti kāmān*  
> *taṃ kāraṇaṃ sāṃkhyayogādhigamyaṃ*  
> *jñātvā devaṃ mucyate sarvapāśaiḥ*
>
> “The one eternal among the many eternals, the one conscious among the
> many conscious, who, being one, grants the desires of the many:
> knowing him, the God who is the cause, to be grasped through Sāṃkhya
> and Yoga, one is freed from all bonds.” (6.13)

Read that first line slowly, because the grammar is doing theology. “The eternal among eternals, the conscious among the conscious.” The God is in the singular, and the beings he stands among are in the plural. The verse asserts, in plain grammatical form, that there are many eternal conscious selves, and one supreme God among them who fulfils their desires. For the philosopher who believes the individual soul is finally identical with the Absolute, this is an awkward sentence. For the philosopher who believes the soul and God are forever distinct, it is a gift.

This is why the verse became a cornerstone for both of the great theistic, difference affirming schools. Rāmānuja, in his *Śrī Bhāṣya*, leans on it to establish that conscious souls are real, many, and eternal, each a distinct mode of the one God. Madhva and the Dvaita tradition go further and read it as scripture’s flat declaration of **Bheda**, eternal difference. Madhva built his whole system on what his followers call the five differences, the eternal distinctions between God and soul, between God and matter, between soul and soul, between soul and matter, and between one piece of matter and another, and the Śvetāśvatara is one of his richest quarries for them. The plurality verse 6.13, the framing of the world as enjoyer and enjoyed and ruler in the first chapter, the two unborn knowing and unknowing selves, all of these the dualist tradition reads as the Upaniṣad saying, in so many words, that you and God are not the same, and never will be.

So here is the irony at the heart of the Śvetāśvatara’s reception, the one specialists know and almost no one else does. This is, on its surface, a Śaiva Upaniṣad. Its supreme God is named Rudra and Hara, the names of Śiva. One scholar has remarked that the Śvetāśvatara served the worship of Śiva much as the Bhagavad Gītā served the worship of Viṣṇu, as its great scriptural charter. And yet the two teachers who quarried it most eagerly for the difference between the soul and God, Rāmānuja and Madhva, were Vaiṣṇavas, worshippers of Viṣṇu, building theologies in which the supreme God is not Śiva at all. An Upaniṣad that names Śiva as the one God became a favorite source of proof texts for the schools devoted to Viṣṇu. The reason is the one we keep returning to. The Śvetāśvatara pitched its deepest claims about God at a level above any single name, and so more than one devotion could come home in it.

## One verse, three Gods

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

If the two birds show the philosophers dividing, there is a single verse that shows the translators dividing, and watching them do so is one of the best ways to understand how alive this Upaniṣad still is.

> *māyāṃ tu prakṛtiṃ vidyān*  
> *māyinaṃ tu maheśvaram*  
> *tasyāvayavabhūtais tu*  
> *vyāptaṃ sarvam idaṃ jagat*
>
> “Know that māyā is prakṛti, nature, and that the wielder of māyā is
> the Great Lord. This whole world is pervaded by beings that are parts
> of him.” (4.10)

The word at the center is **Māyā**. In later Hindu philosophy *māyā* becomes one of the most loaded terms in the language, usually translated as illusion, the cosmic appearance that makes the one reality look like a world of many separate things. But the word is older than that settled meaning, and in the Śvetāśvatara it is doing something the great translators read in three different ways, each reading shaped by the translator’s own sense of God.

Max Müller, the German born Oxford philologist who edited the *Sacred Books of the East* in the nineteenth century, renders *māyā* here as “art” and the Lord as the “maker,” the artist, while admitting in a footnote that the word also carries the sense of illusion, because for the nondual philosophy he favored all the Lord’s making shades into mere appearance. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, the philosopher who became independent India’s second president and whose 1953 *The Principal Upaniṣads* reads the texts as a believing Vedāntin, renders *prakṛti* as *māyā* and calls the Lord “the wielder of *māyā*,” and then insists in his commentary that *māyā* here is not the illusoriness of the world at all but the Lord’s positive creative power, his **śakti**, the real energy by which a real God makes a real world. Patrick Olivelle, in the cooler register of modern critical scholarship, translates it “one should recognize the illusory power as primal matter, and the illusionist as the great Lord,” and then notes carefully that *māyā* here “probably means more a trick or magic than cosmic illusion as in later philosophies that denied the existence of the world.” The scholar Dominic Goodall has made the same point from the philological side, that the *māyā* of the Śvetāśvatara is closer to a creative, supernatural power than to the later doctrine of an unreal universe.

Sit with that for a moment. Three superb readers, one verse, and three different Gods come out the other side. For Müller, schooled in the nonduality of Śaṅkara, the Lord is an artist whose art shades into illusion. For Radhakrishnan, the believing theist, the Lord is a real creator whose *māyā* is his genuine power to bring forth a genuine world. For Olivelle and Goodall, the careful philologists, the Lord is something closer to a magician working a marvel, and the heavy later doctrine of an illusory universe is read back into the verse only by those who came afterward. The Sanskrit sits there on the page, the same four lines, while the God who emerges from them changes with the reader. This is the single best illustration of why the Śvetāśvatara repays slow reading. It is an early text, written before the great systems hardened, and its words still have the openness of that early moment.

## The verse that opened the door to devotion

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

For all its philosophy, the Śvetāśvatara is remembered most for one short verse near its close, because that verse is where Indian scripture speaks, with full clarity, of love for God.

> *yasya deve parā bhaktir*  
> *yathā deve tathā gurau*  
> *tasyaite kathitā hy arthāḥ*  
> *prakāśante mahātmanaḥ*
>
> “These truths, declared here, shine forth only in the great soul who
> has the highest devotion for God, and for the teacher as for God.”
> (6.23)

The word for that highest devotion is **Bhakti**, and this is the only occurrence of the word in the principal Upaniṣads. It is widely regarded as the earliest clear Upaniṣadic statement of loving devotion to a personal God, and it ties that devotion, from the very start, to two things the whole later tradition would keep together: love of God, and reverence for the teacher who reveals him, *yathā deve tathā gurau*, “as toward God, so toward the guru.”

It is hard to overstate how much grows from this small seed. **Bhakti**, loving devotion to a personal God, becomes the central current of Hindu religious life over the following centuries, the force behind the Tamil saints, the great devotional movements that sweep across the subcontinent, the poetry of surrender in a dozen languages. And here it is, already explicit, tied to the love of God and the reverence for the guru, in the closing verse of the Śvetāśvatara. The Upaniṣad even doubles its final words for emphasis, a small liturgical flourish that marks its end, as if the composer knew he had arrived somewhere important. One honest note belongs here, because the careful reader deserves it: Müller observed long ago that this is the single appearance of the word in the text and may belong to its latest layer, an epilogue. Whether or not that is so, the verse sits in the received scripture and became one of the most quoted lines in all of devotional Hinduism.

There is grace here too. The Śvetāśvatara had already said, in the signature verse, that the sage came to know brahman “through the grace of God,” **Devaprasāda**, and earlier still, in that recast verse about the divine size, that the seeker beholds the Lord “by the grace of the Ordainer,” **Dhātuḥ Prasāda**. This is among the earliest clear language of divine grace in the Upaniṣads, the sense that God is not only a truth to be worked out but a person who gives himself to be known. A small scholarly honesty: the line about the grace of the Ordainer is shared with the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, so the Śvetāśvatara is not strictly the first to use it, but the frankly theistic version, the grace of God, the **Devaprasāda** of the signature verse, is its own. Knowledge and love and grace are braided together in this Upaniṣad, and that braid is the devotional religion of India in miniature.

## The Gītā in the distance

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

One last thread ties the Śvetāśvatara to the most beloved scripture of all, and it is the kind of connection a careful reader loves to find.

**Several verses of the Śvetāśvatara stand very close to verses of the Bhagavad Gītā.** The clearest case is the great description of the all pervading being whose limbs are everywhere. The Śvetāśvatara has it at 3.16, “with hands and feet on every side, with eyes and heads and faces on every side, with ears on every side, he stands encompassing all,” and the Bhagavad Gītā, in its thirteenth chapter, has the very same verse, nearly word for word. The seated posture of meditation we read above is shared with the Gītā too, and the whole framework of the field and the knower of the field, of the three **guṇas**, of a personal supreme God who is yet the inner self of all, runs through both.

The relationship is worth stating carefully, because it is easy to get wrong. Both the Śvetāśvatara and the Gītā draw, in this shared verse, on an even older source, a hymn of the Ṛgveda about the god whose eyes and faces are on every side. So the safest way to put it is that both belong to a single emerging theistic stream, the Śvetāśvatara standing at or near its source and the Gītā among its later and fuller flowerings, rather than that one simply copied the other. Olivelle places the Śvetāśvatara just before the formative stage of the Gītā, which fits the picture exactly. When you read the Śvetāśvatara, you are reading the older relative of the Gītā, the place where the personal God of the Gītā is already speaking, in a quieter and more compressed voice.

## Why this small Upaniṣad matters so much

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Step back from the verses and look at what the Śvetāśvatara holds together in six short chapters.

It has the old Upaniṣadic depth, the question of the cause of the world, the identity of the self and the Absolute, the longing to pass beyond death. It has a personal God, one Lord, creator and ruler, hidden in every heart, who can be known and loved. It has the philosophy of its age, the **Sāṃkhya** analysis of nature and the discipline of **Yoga**, taken up and set under that God. It has the oldest seated meditation in the Upaniṣads. It has the word **māyā** poised at the exact moment before it hardened into a single meaning, still open enough that three later theologies could each claim it. It has the two birds, the image on which Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, and Madhva would build three different worlds. It has the plurality verse that the dualists made their banner, and the all genders verse that the devotional heart never tires of, and the paradox of a God who grasps without hands. And it has **Bhakti**, the love of God and the reverence for the teacher, named in scripture for what may be the first time. Almost the entire future of Hindu religious thought is present here, alive and whole.

That is why an Upaniṣad this short has cast a shadow this long. The later traditions found their God already speaking in the Śvetāśvatara, and spent the next two thousand years drawing out what he had said. The personal God of the bhakti saints, the theistic Vedānta of Rāmānuja and Madhva, the meditative practice of the yogins, the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava theologies that shaped the devotional life of a civilization, all of them keep their roots in this one slim, signed, much quoted Upaniṣad. It is the common ancestor, the place where the personal God of Indian devotion stands before the great traditions divided the territory among themselves.

It opened, you remember, with a seminar, a circle of seekers asking where the world comes from and at whose command they live in joy and in pain. By the end it has answered its own question, and the answer is a person. One God, hidden in all beings, the witness in the heart, to be reached by knowledge and by discipline and, in the end, by love. The men in that opening circle wanted to know the cause of things. The Śvetāśvatara told them the cause has a face, and that the face is turned toward them.
